sections.title: Four jobs, one story
sections.content: A longer Hungarian story does four jobs in order, and you now have language for all of them: open it (akkoriban, korábban, amikor + background), move it forward (miután, aztán, eközben, egymás után), mark its turning point (mielőtt, miután and mielőtt together), and close it (végül, az eredmény az volt, hogy, tanulság). A good storyteller doesn't use every tool in every sentence — they pick the right one for the job at hand.

sections.title: The storyteller's toolkit so far
rows: végül, az eredmény az volt, hogy..., tanulság

sections.title: Making it vivid, not just correct
sections.content: Three more words help a well-built story feel alive rather than just grammatically sound: részlet ("a detail") for the small concrete thing that makes a scene real, élénken ("vividly") for describing how something is told or remembered, and folytatás ("continuation, sequel") for signalling more is coming. When you're deciding what to keep and what to cut, ask what the lényeg ("the main point, the gist") of the story actually is — a good story keeps every detail in service of that one thing.

items.spanish: Egy részlet különösen élénken megmaradt bennem.
items.english: One detail stayed vividly in my memory.

items.spanish: Ez még nem a vége — van folytatása is.
items.english: This isn't the end yet — there's a continuation too.

items.spanish: Sok mindent el lehetne mondani, de a lényeg az, hogy végül minden jóra fordult.
items.english: A lot could be said, but the main point is that in the end everything turned out well.

sections.content: When you read your own story back, cut anything that isn't the akkoriban-opening, the miután/mielőtt-sequenced middle, the turning point, or the végül-closing — a few vivid részlet words do more work than a long list of unconnected facts.
